in_text_mentions: The patient reported frequent falls, dysautonomic symptoms including diaphoresis, and mood changes described as emotional lability, depressed affect, and excessive worry. On neurological examination, increased muscle tone was observed along with hypertrophy of the lumbar paravertebral muscles and hyperlordosis, associated with reduced range of motion. Gait assessment revealed a widened base of support, en bloc movement, and impaired turning (Figure 1A and Figure 2A).

On physical examination, increased muscle tone was observed, associated with reduced muscle trophism in the lower limbs, lumbar hyperlordosis, and deformity of the plantar arch and metatarsals of the right foot (Figure 1B and Figure 2B). Paraclinical studies, including thyroid profile, vitamin B12, B1, immunoassay folic acid, and creatine kinase levels (automated enzymatic method), were within normal limits. Serum testing revealed positive GAD antibodies (GAD-Abs) at 98.81 U/mL, while anti-amphiphysin antibodies were negative.

panels.rationale: Single-panel clinical photograph of a real patient showing lateral torso with exaggerated lumbar hyperlordosis and prominently defined, rigid rectus abdominis. Caption and in-text explicitly attribute these findings to stiff-person syndrome (hyperlordosis described as a hallmark clinical sign of SPS). No subtype is specified. Image is grayscale, so skin tone cannot be reliably assessed; no ethnicity or age is stated in the provided text.

Clonus was absent. Muscle power was 5/5 on the right and 4+/5 on the left. Knee jerks were brisk, ankle jerks were normal and the plantar responses were flexor. The sensory examination was normal. Her distribution of stiffness index was 3/6 (number of stiff

She had increased paraspinal muscle tone causing hyperlordosis, which is a hallmark clinical sign of SPS (Fig. 1). The diagnosis in our patient was clinically supported by the characteristic, but not unique, EMG finding of CMUA and the detection of serum GAD-Abs in high titre. GAD-Abs are most commonly detected in type 1 diabetes mellitus (T1DM), which occurs in about 40 % of patients with SPS as seen in our patient, but the titre in T1DM is markedly lower than that of SPS [8]. panels.rationale: Sagittal CT multiplanar reconstruction (MPR-sag) of the spine of the reported stiff-person syndrome patient, showing exaggerated lumbar lordosis measured at 58.35° versus a normal range of 25–45°, directly matching the captioned hyperlordosis of the lumbar spine and the in-text figure reference. This is a real patient image with a visible, disease-specific manifestation of stiff-person syndrome, so it qualifies for inclusion.
panels.attribution_text: Torabi et al. Recurrent Tachycardia, Abdominal, and Chest Pain as a Presentation of Stiff Person Syndrome.. Case reports in medicine 2025. doi:10.1155/carm/4821987. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
in_text_mentions: Babinski reflex was negative. Sensory examination was intact. On his laboratory data, his CK was elevated at the level of 1100 U/L (normal: 53–446 U/L), and his lactate level was increased at 8 mmol/L (normal: less than 2 mmol/L). Because of the increased lactate level, a workup for infectious diseases was done and was negative. The general surgeon did not find any surgical lesion causing his abdominal pain. CT and MRI of the abdomen did not show any intra-abdominal pathology but showed T2 hyperintensities of paraspinal muscles and increased lumbar lordosis at 58° (normal: 25–45°) (Figure 2).

plate_findings.evidence: Significant hyperextension, characteristic stiffness, and marked rigidity of the lower limbs

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Clinical photograph of a patient with anti-GAD-positive stiff person syndrome showing marked lower limb stiffness, hyperextension, and foot deformity; panel is a real patient image and supports an SPS manifestation, though the fixed varus equinus deformity is an unusual/atypical feature. B: Second clinical photograph from the same SPS case shows rigid, abnormally positioned lower limbs and varus equinus foot deformity; on its own it visibly supports a clinical manifestation of the configured disease, with an atypical fixed deformity.
panels.attribution_text: Maarad et al. Stiff Person Syndrome With Positive Anti-glutamic Acid Decarboxylase (GAD) Autoantibodies.. Cureus 2024. doi:10.7759/cureus.67887. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Stiffness of lower limbs with deformities Significant hyperextension, characteristic stiffness, and a varus equinus deformity of the feet. The marked rigidity and abnormal positioning are indicative of the underlying neuromuscular dysfunction associated with her condition, contributing to severe mobility limitations
in_text_mentions: ainful spasms in the lower limbs, leading to significant disability. After nearly a year of symptom progression, she was admitted to our facility. On clinical examination, walking and standing were impossible. Patient exhibited hyperextension of the lower limbs and a varus equinus deformity of the feet (Figure 1). Muscle strength was preserved within the limits of clinical examination, but severe rigidity of the lower limbs and reactive spasms upon touch were present. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the upper limbs, and difficult to evaluate in the lower limbs due to deformity of the feet.
